summary: A model that says 80% should be right about 80% of the time.
headline: Does 80% mean 80%?
overview: Calibration asks whether stated probabilities match reality. Collect everything the model called 70% likely and check how many came true.
A model can rank cases perfectly and still be wildly overconfident. Ranking and honesty are different skills.

break.label: Break it
break.explains: Push the overconfidence up. The reliability curve bends away from the diagonal while AUC stays exactly where it was.

check.question: A model's AUC is high but its reliability curve is far from the diagonal. What is true?
options: It ranks well but its percentages are not trustworthy

realLife: Risk scores that drive decisions, such as who gets an intervention, need honest percentages, not just good ordering.
data: Three thousand cases with a known true probability. The model's stated probability is a stretched or squashed version of the truth. Everything is measured on 1,500 cases; the recalibration step is fitted on the other 1,500.
maths: ECE = Σ (share in bin) × |mean predicted − observed rate|
A strictly increasing change to the probabilities leaves AUC unchanged.
Recalibration here is Platt scaling: a one-feature logistic regression on the logit of the score.
code:
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV, calibration_curve
cal = CalibratedClassifierCV(model, method='sigmoid', cv=3).fit(Xtr, ytr)
calibration_curve(yte, cal.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1], n_bins=10)
